content: Extramammary Paget's disease is a rare type of superficial skin cancer, most commonly affecting the vulva. It predominantly occurs in postmenopausal white women. This disease often spreads in a hidden manner, with its margins extending beyond the visible edges of the lesion. Treatment options range from surgical interventions to non-invasive techniques. The primary challenge in managing this condition is to effectively treat or remove the disease, including areas that may not be visibly affected, while avoiding overtreatment and minimizing complications associated with radical surgery. Currently, there is no clear consensus on the optimal treatment approach. Surgery remains the most commonly employed method, but it is difficult to completely excise the disease, and recurrence is frequent. This often necessitates repeated surgeries, which can lead to significant anatomical damage. Alternative treatments, such as photodynamic therapy, laser therapy, radiotherapy, topical treatments, and chemotherapy, have been proposed. It is crucial to evaluate the evidence supporting these alternatives, particularly newer cell-specific treatments like photodynamic therapy and imiquimod, to determine if they can reduce the need for radical surgical procedures. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and risks of various treatment modalities for managing Paget's disease of the vulva. A comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and Embase, was conducted up to May 8, 2018. Additional searches included clinical trial registries, scientific meeting abstracts, and reference lists of review articles. The review aimed to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and well-designed non-randomized studies comparing different interventions for this condition. Despite an extensive search, no trials meeting the inclusion criteria were found. The original review identified 635 unique references, and 31 full-text articles were assessed, but all were excluded for not meeting the criteria. However, a narrative account of studies involving more than 10 women was included, as this represents the only available evidence base for this rare disease. Surgery remains the primary treatment modality in the literature, with other treatments limited to case reports or used for inoperable or recurrent cases. Between September 2013 and May 2018, 35 new studies were identified, but none met the inclusion criteria. One prospective study of good quality investigated the use of 5% imiquimod cream in eight women with recurrent Paget's disease of the vulva. Although small in scale, this study demonstrated promising results. Additionally, a prospective trial involving 20 women was anticipated to be reported. The authors concluded that since the last review, there has been an increase in reports documenting clinical responses to 5% imiquimod cream. The growing evidence for the safety and efficacy of this treatment is encouraging for both patients and clinicians. While a multicenter RCT of adequate size is ideally needed, ongoing high-quality non-randomized prospective studies will continue to enhance the current body of literature.
